16  Eigenvalue Problems and the QR Algorithm

The eigenvalue problem \(\bA\bv = \lambda\bv\) identifies the invariant one-dimensional subspaces of a linear operator. Along an eigenvector \(\bv\), the action of the matrix \(\bA\) reduces to scalar scaling by \(\lambda\). Eigenvalues govern the asymptotic stability of dynamical systems, the resonant frequencies of mechanical and electrical systems, the convergence rates of iterative solvers, and the dominant invariant coordinates in spectral graph theory and data science.

The characteristic equation \(\det(\bA-\lambda\bI)=0\) is useful for definitions and very small examples, but forming its coefficients is not a sound numerical algorithm. It discards the matrix structure and replaces one problem by a polynomial root problem that may be far more sensitive. Practical methods work with the matrix directly and use orthogonal or unitary transformations whenever possible.

16.1 Invariant Directions and Change of Basis

NoteDefinition: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

Let \(\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}\). A nonzero vector \(\bv \in \fC^n\) is an eigenvector of \(\bA\) associated with eigenvalue \(\lambda \in \fC\) if \[ \begin{align} \bA\bv = \lambda\bv. \end{align} \] The set of eigenvalues is the spectrum \(\sigma(\bA)\). When eigenvalues are listed as \(\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n\), repetitions are included according to algebraic multiplicity.

NoteDefinition: Invariant Subspace

A subspace \(S\subseteq\fC^n\) is invariant under \(\bA\) if \(\bA\bx\in S\) whenever \(\bx\in S\). An eigenvector spans a one-dimensional invariant subspace. Higher-dimensional invariant subspaces remain meaningful even when no basis of eigenvectors exists.

NoteExample

Three two-dimensional examples show what the definition can and cannot promise.

  1. A diagonal matrix scales the coordinate axes, leaving both axes invariant.

  2. The shear \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has only one independent eigenvector. Repeated application keeps sliding vectors in the same direction, so a repeated eigenvalue need not supply a full eigenbasis.

  3. A nontrivial planar rotation has no real invariant line, but it has complex eigenvectors. Complex numbers are not an artificial complication here: they encode rotation as multiplication by a complex phase.

NoteDefinition: Similarity and a Change of Basis

Matrices \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) are similar if \[ \begin{align} \bB=\bS^{-1}\bA\bS \end{align} \] for some nonsingular \(\bS\). They represent the same linear map in different bases: the columns of \(\bS\) are the new basis vectors written in the old coordinates.

NoteTheorem: Similarity Preserves Eigenvalues

If \(\bB=\bS^{-1}\bA\bS\), then \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) have the same eigenvalues. More precisely, \(\bA\bv=\lambda\bv\) if and only if \[ \begin{align} \bB(\bS^{-1}\bv)=\lambda(\bS^{-1}\bv). \end{align} \]

TipProof

Multiplying \(\bA\bv=\lambda\bv\) by \(\bS^{-1}\) and inserting \(\bS\bS^{-1}=\bI\) gives \[ \begin{align} (\bS^{-1}\bA\bS)(\bS^{-1}\bv) =\lambda(\bS^{-1}\bv). \end{align} \] The reverse implication follows by multiplying by \(\bS\).

NoteTheorem: Diagonalization Means an Eigenvector Basis

A matrix \(\bA\in\fC^{n\times n}\) is similar to a diagonal matrix if and only if it has a basis of eigenvectors. If \(\bS=(\bv_1\ \cdots\ \bv_n)\) contains such a basis, then \[ \begin{align} \bA\bS=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}, \qquad \bA=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bS^{-1}. \end{align} \]

TipProof

If the columns of \(\bS\) are eigenvectors, the \(j\)th columns of \(\bA\bS\) and \(\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\) are both \(\lambda_j\bv_j\), which proves the factorization. Conversely, if \(\bA=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bS^{-1}\), then \(\bA\bS=\bS\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\), so each column of the nonsingular matrix \(\bS\) is an eigenvector.

16.2 Multiplicity and Schur Form

NoteDefinition: Algebraic and Geometric Multiplicity

Let \(\lambda\) be an eigenvalue of \(\bA\).

  1. The algebraic multiplicity \(\mu_a(\lambda)\) is the multiplicity of \(\lambda\) as a root of \(\det(\bA - z\bI) = 0\).

  2. The geometric multiplicity \(\mu_g(\lambda) = \dim \mathcal{N}(\bA - \lambda\bI)\) is the dimension of the corresponding eigenspace.

Every eigenvalue satisfies \(1 \leq \mu_g(\lambda) \leq \mu_a(\lambda)\). When \(\mu_g(\lambda) < \mu_a(\lambda)\) for any eigenvalue, \(\bA\) is defective and does not possess a complete basis of eigenvectors.

NoteTheorem: Schur Triangularization Decomposition

Every square matrix \(\bA \in \fC^{n \times n}\) is unitarily similar to an upper triangular matrix: \[ \begin{align} \bA = \bQ\bT\bQ^*, \end{align} \] where \(\bQ \in \fC^{n \times n}\) is unitary (\(\bQ^*\bQ = \bI\)) and \(\bT \in \fC^{n \times n}\) is upper triangular. The diagonal entries of \(\bT\) are the eigenvalues of \(\bA\).

TipProof

We proceed by induction on the matrix dimension \(n\). For \(n = 1\), the statement holds trivially with \(\bQ = [1]\) and \(\bT = \bA\).

Assume the theorem holds for all square matrices of order \(n - 1\). By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, the characteristic polynomial \(\det(\bA - z\bI) = 0\) possesses at least one complex root \(\lambda_1\). Let \(\bv_1 \in \fC^n\) be an eigenvector associated with \(\lambda_1\), normalized so that \(\|\bv_1\|_2 = 1\). Using the Gram–Schmidt process or Householder reflectors, construct an orthonormal basis for \(\fC^n\) whose first column is \(\bv_1\), forming a unitary matrix \(\bU_1 = [\bv_1, \bW] \in \fC^{n \times n}\) with \(\bW \in \fC^{n \times (n-1)}\).

Applying this unitary similarity transformation to \(\bA\) gives \[ \begin{align} \bU_1^* \bA \bU_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \bv_1^* \\ \bW^* \end{pmatrix} \bA \begin{pmatrix} \bv_1 & \bW \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \bv_1^* \bA \bv_1 & \bv_1^* \bA \bW \\ \bW^* \bA \bv_1 & \bW^* \bA \bW \end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \] Because \(\bA\bv_1 = \lambda_1 \bv_1\), the leading entry is \(\bv_1^*(\lambda_1\bv_1) = \lambda_1 \|\bv_1\|_2^2 = \lambda_1\). The lower-left block is \(\bW^*(\lambda_1\bv_1) = \lambda_1(\bW^*\bv_1) = \bzero\), because the columns of \(\bW\) are orthogonal to \(\bv_1\). Thus \[ \begin{align} \bU_1^* \bA \bU_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bw^* \\ \bzero & \bA_1 \end{pmatrix}, \end{align} \] where \(\bA_1 = \bW^* \bA \bW \in \fC^{(n-1) \times (n-1)}\) and \(\bw^* = \bv_1^* \bA \bW\).

By the induction hypothesis, there exists a unitary matrix \(\bQ_1 \in \fC^{(n-1) \times (n-1)}\) such that \(\bQ_1^* \bA_1 \bQ_1 = \bT_1\) is upper triangular. Define the \(n \times n\) block-diagonal unitary matrix \[ \begin{align} \bV = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \bzero \\ \bzero & \bQ_1 \end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \] Setting \(\bQ = \bU_1 \bV\), which is unitary as the product of unitary matrices, we obtain \[ \begin{align} \bQ^* \bA \bQ = \bV^* (\bU_1^* \bA \bU_1) \bV = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \bzero \\ \bzero & \bQ_1^* \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bw^* \\ \bzero & \bA_1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \bzero \\ \bzero & \bQ_1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bw^* \bQ_1 \\ \bzero & \bQ_1^* \bA_1 \bQ_1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bw^* \bQ_1 \\ \bzero & \bT_1 \end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \] Because \(\bT_1\) is upper triangular, the entire block matrix \(\bT = \bQ^*\bA\bQ\) is upper triangular. The diagonal entries of \(\bT\) are \(\lambda_1\) and the eigenvalues of \(\bA_1\), which collectively form the eigenvalues of \(\bA\).

NoteTheorem: Spectral Theorem for Real Symmetric Matrices

If \(\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}\) is real symmetric (\(\bA = \bA^T\)), then all eigenvalues of \(\bA\) are real, and \(\bA\) is orthogonally diagonalizable: \[ \begin{align} \bA = \bQ \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bQ^T = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \bq_i \bq_i^T, \end{align} \] where \(\bQ \in \fR^{n \times n}\) is real orthogonal (\(\bQ^T\bQ = \bI\)) and \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_n)\) is real diagonal.

TipProof

First, let \(\lambda \in \fC\) and \(\bv \in \fC^n \setminus \{\bzero\}\) satisfy \(\bA\bv = \lambda\bv\). Taking the inner product with \(\bv\), \[ \begin{align} \bv^*\bA\bv = \bv^*(\lambda\bv) = \lambda\|\bv\|_2^2. \end{align} \] Taking the conjugate transpose of this scalar and using \(\bA = \bA^T = \bA^*\), \[ \begin{align} \bv^*\bA\bv = (\bv^*\bA\bv)^* = (\lambda\|\bv\|_2^2)^* = \bar{\lambda}\|\bv\|_2^2. \end{align} \] Subtracting these two scalar expressions gives \[ \begin{align} (\lambda - \bar{\lambda})\|\bv\|_2^2 = 0. \end{align} \] Because \(\bv \neq \bzero\), \(\|\bv\|_2^2 > 0\), forcing \(\lambda = \bar{\lambda} \in \fR\). Thus all eigenvalues are real.

Because \(\lambda_1 \in \fR\) and \(\bA\) is real, writing \(\bv = \bx + i\by\) gives \(\bA\bx = \lambda_1\bx\) and \(\bA\by = \lambda_1\by\). At least one of \(\bx,\by\) is nonzero, yielding a real unit eigenvector \(\bq_1\). Extend \(\bq_1\) to an orthogonal matrix \(\bQ_1 = [\bq_1, \bW] \in \fR^{n \times n}\) with \(\bW \in \fR^{n \times (n-1)}\). Because \(\bA\bq_1 = \lambda_1\bq_1\) and \(\bW^T\bq_1 = \bzero\): \[ \begin{align} \bQ_1^T\bA\bQ_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \bq_1^T \\ \bW^T \end{pmatrix} \bA \begin{pmatrix} \bq_1 & \bW \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \bq_1^T\bA\bq_1 & \bq_1^T\bA\bW \\ \bW^T\bA\bq_1 & \bW^T\bA\bW \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & (\bW^T\bA\bq_1)^T \\ \bzero & \bA_1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & \bzero^T \\ \bzero & \bA_1 \end{pmatrix}, \end{align} \] where \(\bA_1 = \bW^T\bA\bW \in \fR^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}\) is symmetric. By induction on dimension, there exists an orthogonal \(\bQ_2 \in \fR^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}\) such that \(\bQ_2^T\bA_1\bQ_2 = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_2, ..., \lambda_n)\). The matrix \[ \begin{align} \bQ = \bQ_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \bzero \\ \bzero & \bQ_2 \end{pmatrix} \end{align} \] is orthogonal and satisfies \(\bQ^T\bA\bQ = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\), so \(\bA = \bQ\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\bQ^T\).

NoteTheorem: Courant–Fischer Minimax Theorem

Let \(\bA \in \fR^{n \times n}\) be real symmetric with eigenvalues ordered as \(\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq ... \leq \lambda_n\). Then for each \(k \in \{1, ..., n\}\), \[ \begin{align} \lambda_k = \min_{\dim(S) = k} \max_{\bx \in S,\, \bx \neq \bzero} \frac{\bx^T \bA \bx}{\bx^T \bx} = \max_{\dim(S) = n - k + 1} \min_{\bx \in S,\, \bx \neq \bzero} \frac{\bx^T \bA \bx}{\bx^T \bx}. \end{align} \]

TipProof

Let \(\bq_1, ..., \bq_n\) be an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \(\bA\) with \(\bA\bq_i = \lambda_i \bq_i\). For any nonzero \(\bx = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \bq_i\), the Rayleigh quotient satisfies \[ \begin{align} R(\bx) = \frac{\bx^T\bA\bx}{\bx^T\bx} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2}. \end{align} \] Define the subspace \(V_k = \operatorname{span}\{\bq_1, ..., \bq_k\}\), which has dimension \(k\). For any nonzero \(\bx \in V_k\), \(c_i = 0\) for all \(i > k\), so \[ \begin{align} R(\bx) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^2} \leq \lambda_k \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i^2} = \lambda_k. \end{align} \] Because \(\bq_k \in V_k\) achieves \(R(\bq_k) = \lambda_k\), we have \(\max_{\bx \in V_k,\, \bx \neq \bzero} R(\bx) = \lambda_k\).

Now let \(S\) be any arbitrary subspace of \(\fR^n\) with \(\dim(S) = k\). Define \(W_{k-1} = \operatorname{span}\{\bq_k, ..., \bq_n\}\), which has dimension \(n - k + 1\). By the dimension formula, \[ \begin{align} \dim(S \cap W_{k-1}) = \dim(S) + \dim(W_{k-1}) - \dim(S + W_{k-1}) \geq k + (n - k + 1) - n = 1. \end{align} \] Therefore, there exists a nonzero vector \(\by \in S \cap W_{k-1}\). Because \(\by \in W_{k-1}\), its expansion \(\by = \sum_{i=k}^n d_i \bq_i\) contains only modes \(i \geq k\), so \[ \begin{align} R(\by) = \frac{\sum_{i=k}^n \lambda_i d_i^2}{\sum_{i=k}^n d_i^2} \geq \lambda_k \frac{\sum_{i=k}^n d_i^2}{\sum_{i=k}^n d_i^2} = \lambda_k. \end{align} \] Because \(\by \in S\), the maximum over \(S\) satisfies \(\max_{\bx \in S,\, \bx \neq \bzero} R(\bx) \geq R(\by) \geq \lambda_k\). Taking the minimum over all \(k\)-dimensional subspaces \(S\) proves the first equality. The dual maximum-minimum characterization follows similarly by replacing \(\bA\) with \(-\bA\).

NoteTheorem: Cauchy Interlacing Theorem

Let \(\bA\in\fR^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and let \(\bB\in\fR^{(n-1)\times(n-1)}\) be a principal submatrix. If \[ \begin{align} \lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n, \qquad \mu_1\leq\cdots\leq\mu_{n-1} \end{align} \] are the eigenvalues of \(\bA\) and \(\bB\), respectively, then \[ \begin{align} \lambda_k\leq\mu_k\leq\lambda_{k+1}, \qquad k=1,...,n-1. \end{align} \]

TipProof

After a simultaneous permutation of rows and columns, we may assume that \(\bB\) is obtained by deleting the last row and column. Identify \(\fR^{n-1}\) with the coordinate hyperplane \[ \begin{align} H=\{\bx\in\fR^n:x_n=0\}. \end{align} \] For every nonzero \(\bx\in H\), the Rayleigh quotients of \(\bA\) and \(\bB\) agree.

Apply the first Courant–Fischer characterization from the result above. The minimization defining \(\mu_k\) ranges only over \(k\)-dimensional subspaces of \(H\), whereas the minimization defining \(\lambda_k\) ranges over all \(k\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\fR^n\). Restricting the admissible set cannot decrease the minimum, so \(\lambda_k\leq\mu_k\).

For the other inequality, use the dual characterization. Since \(\dim(H)=n-1\), \[ \begin{align} \mu_k &=\max_{\substack{S\subset H\\ \dim(S)=n-k}} \min_{\bx\in S,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R_{\bA}(\bx) \leq\max_{\substack{S\subset\fR^n\\ \dim(S)=n-k}} \min_{\bx\in S,\,\bx\neq\bzero}R_{\bA}(\bx) =\lambda_{k+1}. \end{align} \] Together the two bounds give the interlacing inequalities.

16.3 Power Iteration and Shifted Inverse Iteration

NoteDefinition: Power Iteration

Let \(\bA\) be real symmetric. Given a unit vector \(\bv^{(0)}\), power iteration constructs \[ \begin{align} \bw^{(k)} = \bA \bv^{(k-1)}, \qquad \bv^{(k)} = \frac{\bw^{(k)}}{\|\bw^{(k)}\|_2}, \qquad \lambda^{(k)} = (\bv^{(k)})^T \bA \bv^{(k)}. \end{align} \] Order the eigenvalues by magnitude. If \(|\lambda_1|>|\lambda_2|\geq\cdots\geq|\lambda_n|\) and \(\bq_1^T\bv^{(0)}\neq0\), the direction of the iterate converges linearly: \[ \begin{align} \|\bv^{(k)} - (\pm \bq_1)\|_2 = O\left( \left| \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} \right|^k \right). \end{align} \] For a general nonnormal matrix, an eigenvector basis may be poorly conditioned or may not exist, and this simple orthogonal expansion no longer justifies the claim.

NoteDefinition: Shifted Inverse Iteration

For a real symmetric matrix, an eigenvalue near a target \(\sigma\) can be isolated by applying power iteration implicitly to \((\bA-\sigma\bI)^{-1}\): \[ \begin{align} (\bA - \sigma \bI) \bw^{(k)} = \bv^{(k-1)}, \qquad \bv^{(k)} = \frac{\bw^{(k)}}{\|\bw^{(k)}\|_2}. \end{align} \] The eigenvalues of \((\bA - \sigma \bI)^{-1}\) are \((\lambda_i - \sigma)^{-1}\). Provided the shift is not itself an eigenvalue and the starting vector contains the desired component, the mode closest to \(\sigma\) dominates. The matrix inverse is never formed: each step solves a shifted linear system.

NoteDefinition: Rayleigh Quotient Iteration (RQI)

For symmetric matrices, updating the shift dynamically to the current Rayleigh estimate \(\sigma_k = (\bv^{(k)})^T \bA \bv^{(k)}\) defines Rayleigh Quotient Iteration: \[ \begin{align} (\bA - \sigma_k \bI) \bw^{(k+1)} = \bv^{(k)}, \qquad \bv^{(k+1)} = \frac{\bw^{(k+1)}}{\|\bw^{(k+1)}\|_2}, \qquad \sigma_{k+1} = (\bv^{(k+1)})^T \bA \bv^{(k+1)}. \end{align} \]

NoteTheorem: Local Cubic Convergence of Rayleigh Quotient Iteration

Let \(\bA\) be real symmetric, and let \(\lambda_*\) be a simple eigenvalue with unit eigenvector \(\bq_*\). If a unit RQI iterate \(\bv^{(k)}\) is sufficiently close to \(\bq_*\), then \[ \begin{align} \sin\angle(\bv^{(k+1)},\bq_*) \leq C\sin^3\angle(\bv^{(k)},\bq_*). \end{align} \] If \(\lambda_*\) is an extremal eigenvalue, the Rayleigh shifts also satisfy \[ \begin{align} |\sigma_{k+1}-\lambda_*| \leq C'|\sigma_k-\lambda_*|^3 \end{align} \] for iterates sufficiently close to \(\bq_*\).

TipProof

Write the current unit vector as \[ \begin{align} \bv=\cos\theta\,\bq_*+\sin\theta\,\bz, \qquad \bz\perp\bq_*, \qquad \|\bz\|_2=1. \end{align} \] Its Rayleigh quotient \(\sigma=\bv^T\bA\bv\) obeys \[ \begin{align} \sigma &= (\cos\theta\,\bq_*+\sin\theta\,\bz)^T\bA(\cos\theta\,\bq_*+\sin\theta\,\bz) \\ &= \cos^2\theta\,\lambda_* + 2\cos\theta\sin\theta\,\bq_*^T\bA\bz + \sin^2\theta\,\bz^T\bA\bz. \end{align} \] Because \(\bA\bq_* = \lambda_*\bq_*\) and \(\bq_*^T\bz = 0\), the cross-term vanishes: \(\bq_*^T\bA\bz = \lambda_*\bq_*^T\bz = 0\). Substituting \(\cos^2\theta = 1-\sin^2\theta\), \[ \begin{align} \sigma-\lambda_* = (1-\sin^2\theta)\lambda_* + \sin^2\theta\,\bz^T\bA\bz - \lambda_* = \sin^2\theta\,(\bz^T\bA\bz-\lambda_*), \end{align} \] so \(|\sigma-\lambda_*|\leq C_0\sin^2\theta\).

Let \(\gamma=\min_{\lambda_j\neq\lambda_*}|\lambda_j-\lambda_*|>0\). Once \(\theta\) is small enough, \(|\lambda_j-\sigma|\geq\gamma/2\) for every other eigenvalue. Expanding the inverse-iteration vector \(\bw=(\bA-\sigma\bI)^{-1}\bv\) in an orthonormal eigenbasis, its component along \(\bq_*\) has magnitude \[ \begin{align} \frac{|\cos\theta|}{|\lambda_*-\sigma|}, \end{align} \] whereas the norm of its orthogonal component is at most \(2|\sin\theta|/\gamma\). Normalization does not change their ratio. Therefore, \[ \begin{align} \tan\angle(\bv^+,\bq_*) \leq \frac{2|\lambda_*-\sigma|}{\gamma|\cos\theta|}|\sin\theta| \leq C_1|\sin\theta|^3. \end{align} \] For small angles, \(\sin\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) are comparable, which proves cubic convergence of the eigenvector direction.

If \(\lambda_*\) is extremal, the spectral gap also gives two-sided local bounds \(c\sin^2\theta\leq|\sigma-\lambda_*|\leq C\sin^2\theta\). Applying the Rayleigh-quotient identity to the next iterate and using the cubic angle bound yields \[ \begin{align} |\sigma^+-\lambda_*| \leq C_2\sin^2\angle(\bv^+,\bq_*) \leq C_3\sin^6\theta \leq C_4|\sigma-\lambda_*|^3. \end{align} \]

16.4 The Practical QR Algorithm

NoteDefinition: Basic QR Iteration

Given \(\bA_0 = \bA\), the unshifted QR iteration generates orthogonally similar matrices via \[ \begin{align} \bA_k = \bQ_k \bR_k, \qquad \bA_{k+1} = \bR_k \bQ_k = \bQ_k^T \bA_k \bQ_k. \end{align} \] All iterates share the same eigenvalues. Under suitable separation conditions the subdiagonal entries tend to zero and the iterates reveal a Schur form. Shifts and deflation are essential for a reliable practical method.

NoteLemma: Invariance of Hessenberg Structure under QR Iteration

Let \(\bH \in \fR^{n \times n}\) be an upper Hessenberg matrix (\(H_{ij} = 0\) for all \(i > j + 1\)). If \(\bH = \bQ\bR\) is the QR factorization of \(\bH\), then the reversed product \(\bH_+ = \bR\bQ\) is also upper Hessenberg.

TipProof

Because \(\bH = \bQ\bR\) and \(\bR\) is upper triangular and invertible (assuming \(\bH\) is nonsingular, or extending by continuity), \(\bQ = \bH \bR^{-1}\). Because the inverse of an upper triangular matrix is upper triangular, \(\bR^{-1}\) is upper triangular. The product of an upper Hessenberg matrix \(\bH\) and an upper triangular matrix \(\bR^{-1}\) is upper Hessenberg. Therefore, \(\bQ\) is upper Hessenberg.

Now consider \(\bH_+ = \bR\bQ\). The matrix \(\bR\) is upper triangular and \(\bQ\) is upper Hessenberg. For entry \((i, j)\) with \(i > j + 1\): \[ \begin{align} (\bH_+)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^n R_{ik} Q_{kj}. \end{align} \] Because \(\bR\) is upper triangular, \(R_{ik} = 0\) for all \(k < i\). For the remaining terms \(k \geq i\), we have \(k \geq i > j + 1\), which implies \(k > j + 1\). Because \(\bQ\) is upper Hessenberg, \(Q_{kj} = 0\) for all \(k > j + 1\). Thus every term in the sum vanishes, proving \((\bH_+)_{ij} = 0\) for \(i > j + 1\).

NoteTheorem: Practical Shifted QR Framework

A standard dense nonsymmetric eigenvalue computation has two phases:

  1. Hessenberg reduction: Compute \(\bH_0=\bU_0^T\bA\bU_0\) with Householder reflectors. This one-time reduction costs \(O(n^3)\) operations and preserves the eigenvalues.

  2. Implicit shifted QR steps: Apply shifts while preserving Hessenberg form. A schematic single-shift step is \[ \begin{align} \bH_k - \mu_k \bI = \bQ_k \bR_k, \qquad \bH_{k+1} = \bR_k \bQ_k + \mu_k \bI. \end{align} \] Lem.~above explains why each step costs \(O(n^2)\) rather than \(O(n^3)\). Real nonsymmetric codes use implicit single or double shifts so that complex conjugate pairs can remain in real arithmetic. A small subdiagonal entry permits deflation and splits the problem into smaller blocks.

For a real symmetric matrix, Hessenberg form reduces to tridiagonal form. Wilkinson shifts from the trailing two by two block and implicit bulge chasing then give a particularly efficient symmetric algorithm.

16.5 Exercises

WarningExercise

  1. Derive. (Rayleigh quotient stationary points) For a real symmetric matrix \(\bA\), define the Rayleigh quotient \(R(\bx) = \frac{\bx^T\bA\bx}{\bx^T\bx}\) on \(\fR^n \setminus \{\bzero\}\).

    1. Compute the gradient \(\nabla R(\bx)\) directly.

    2. Prove that \(\nabla R(\bx) = \bzero\) if and only if \(\bx\) is an eigenvector of \(\bA\).

    3. Restrict the Hessian \(\nabla^2R(\bq_i)\) to directions orthogonal to \(\bq_i\). Show that its eigenvalues on this tangent space are \(\frac{2}{\|\bq_i\|_2^2}(\lambda_j-\lambda_i)\) for \(j\neq i\). Explain why the radial direction has zero curvature, and conclude that the smallest and largest eigenvalues are the global extrema of \(R\).

  2. Derive. (Similarity is a coordinate change) Choose a nonorthogonal basis of \(\fR^2\), form its basis matrix \(\bS\), and compute \(\bS^{-1}\bA\bS\) for a simple diagonal matrix \(\bA\). Verify directly that eigenvalues are preserved although lengths and angles generally are not.

  3. Explore. (A defective shear) For \(\bA=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), find the algebraic and geometric multiplicities of the eigenvalue. Compute \(\bA^k\) and explain how its growth is invisible if one records only the eigenvalue \(1\).

  4. Compute. (Observed cubic convergence of RQI) Apply RQI to a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues, starting from several unit vectors close to the same eigenvector.

    1. Record the angle errors \(\theta_k=\angle(\bv^{(k)},\bq_*)\) and the ratios \(\sin\theta_{k+1}/\sin^3\theta_k\).

    2. Record the Rayleigh errors and verify the cubic relation in the result above before rounding error dominates.

    3. Repeat with two nearly repeated eigenvalues and explain how the spectral gap enters the constants in the proof.

  5. Compute. (Cauchy interlacing on a concrete matrix) For \[ \begin{align} \bA=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&2&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}, \end{align} \] compute the eigenvalues of \(\bA\) and of the leading \(2\times2\) principal submatrix. Verify each inequality in the result above. Repeat after deleting the middle row and column.

  6. Explore. (Failure of unshifted QR on an exchange matrix) Let \(\bP = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\).

    1. Compute the QR factorization \(\bP = \bQ_0 \bR_0\).

    2. Compute \(\bP_1 = \bR_0 \bQ_0\) and show that \(\bP_1 = \bP\).

    3. Repeat the step with a nonzero shift. Determine which shifts break the cycle, and explain how an eigenvalue shift from the trailing two by two block permits immediate deflation in this example.

  7. Compute. (Givens rotation Hessenberg QR) Write a Python function that executes one step of shifted QR on an upper Hessenberg matrix \(\bH \in \fR^{n \times n}\) using \(n-1\) Givens rotations. Verify that your implementation requires \(O(n^2)\) flops rather than \(O(n^3)\).
